content: Scoliosis is a medical condition characterized by an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine, often described as an “S” or “C” shaped curve when viewed from behind. It primarily affects the thoracic and lumbar regions of the spine. The curvature can range from mild to severe and may be associated with rotation of the vertebrae. Mechanistically, scoliosis involves three-dimensional deformities of the spine and can result from a variety of underlying causes including idiopathic origin (unknown cause), congenital spine malformations, neuromuscular conditions, or degenerative diseases. The most common form, adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, develops during the growth spurt before puberty. Clinically, scoliosis may present with uneven shoulders or hips, visible spinal curvature, back pain, or sometimes no symptoms. Evaluation typically involves clinical examination and radiographic imaging like X-rays to measure the Cobb angle, which quantifies curve severity. Management strategies depend on the severity and progression risk and include observation, bracing, physical therapy, and in some cases, surgery. Lifestyle modifications focusing on posture, physical activity, and ergonomic adjustments can improve comfort and function. Major synonyms include spinal curvature and lateral spinal curvature. Limitations in current understanding pertain mainly to idiopathic scoliosis causes and variable treatment outcomes. Safety considerations address risks of untreated severe scoliosis such as respiratory compromise and chronic pain, while surgical interventions carry procedure-specific risks. Evidence ranges from well-established diagnostic criteria and treatment protocols to emerging research on genetic and biomechanical factors.

content: Scoliosis is defined as an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine greater than 10 degrees, measured by the Cobb angle on spinal X-rays. It is classified into different types based on etiology: idiopathic (most common, unknown cause), congenital (due to vertebral malformations at birth), neuromuscular (associated with disorders like cerebral palsy or muscular dystrophy), and degenerative (related to aging and spinal degeneration). Each classification has distinct pathophysiological mechanisms influencing clinical presentation and prognosis. The angle and location of the curve help guide classification and treatment planning.

content: The causes of scoliosis vary widely. Idiopathic scoliosis, which accounts for approximately 80% of cases, has no definitive known cause but is believed to involve genetic, hormonal, and biomechanical factors affecting spinal growth and symmetry. Congenital scoliosis results from abnormal vertebral development in utero. Neuromuscular scoliosis arises from muscle imbalance and poor spinal support due to neurological conditions. Degenerative scoliosis develops due to asymmetric wear and tear on spinal joints and discs in older adults. Mechanistically, scoliosis involves complex three-dimensional deformation including lateral curve, vertebral rotation, and changes in the sagittal profile.

content: Scoliosis affects about 2-3% of adolescents, with idiopathic scoliosis being the most prevalent form. Females are more likely to experience curve progression. Risk factors include family history, rapid growth during puberty, certain neuromuscular conditions, and congenital spine abnormalities. Although scoliosis can appear at any age, the adolescent growth spurt is a critical period for progression. Early identification of high-risk individuals allows timely monitoring and intervention to prevent severe deformity.

content: Many individuals with scoliosis have no symptoms in mild cases. Visible signs include uneven shoulders or waist, prominence of ribs on one side, and uneven hips. Back pain is more common in adult degenerative scoliosis but can occur in adolescents. Severe curves may lead to difficulty breathing due to reduced chest wall compliance. Neurological symptoms such as numbness or weakness are rare but may indicate spinal cord involvement. Clinical examination focuses on posture assessment and the Adam’s forward bend test to reveal asymmetry.

content: Diagnosis begins with a detailed history and physical examination, including assessment of spinal curvature, shoulder and pelvic alignment, and neurological status. The Adam’s forward bend test is a screening tool for detecting rib humps indicative of rotation. Radiographic evaluation with standing full-spine X-rays is essential to measure the Cobb angle, assess curve pattern, and monitor progression. Advanced imaging like MRI is indicated when neurological signs are present or congenital anomalies are suspected. The Cobb angle classification guides treatment decisions.

content: Management depends on curve severity and risk of progression. Observation with regular follow-up is standard for mild curves (<25 degrees) in growing children. Bracing is recommended for moderate curves (25-45 degrees) to prevent progression. Physical therapy can support postural strength and flexibility but does not typically alter curve progression. Surgical intervention, such as spinal fusion, is considered for severe curves (>45-50 degrees), progressive deformity, or when respiratory compromise occurs. Emerging treatments include vertebral body tethering for select patients.

content: People with scoliosis should maintain an active lifestyle tailored to their condition. Physical activity helps preserve spinal mobility and muscle strength. Activities like swimming, walking, and yoga can be beneficial, while contact sports may require caution depending on severity. Ergonomic adjustments in daily activities, including proper seating and sleeping positions, can reduce discomfort. Weight management is important, especially in degenerative scoliosis, to minimize additional spinal stress. Psychological support may be necessary due to body image concerns.

content: Untreated severe scoliosis can lead to progressive deformity causing chronic back pain, spinal instability, and restrictive lung disease due to impaired chest wall expansion. Cardiac dysfunction is rare but possible in extreme cases. Neurological complications such as spinal cord compression are uncommon but necessitate urgent intervention. Psychosocial impacts include reduced self-esteem and activity limitation. Regular monitoring is vital to detect deterioration early and apply appropriate treatment to limit complications.

content: A common misconception is that scoliosis is always painful; in many cases, especially mild scoliosis, pain is absent. Another is that poor posture causes scoliosis; however, scoliosis is a structural spinal deformity not caused by posture habits. Some believe scoliosis uniformly requires surgery, while many mild cases do not. The idea that scoliosis in adults always stems from childhood scoliosis is incorrect; degenerative scoliosis can develop later in life. Treatment efficacy varies, and no single approach fits all cases.

content: Safety considerations during scoliosis treatment involve minimizing risks related to bracing and surgery. Braces can cause skin irritation; compliance is critical for effectiveness. Radiation exposure from serial imaging should be minimized with appropriate protocols. Regular clinical and radiographic follow-up ensures timely adjustment of management plans based on curve behavior and symptom development.
